### A.2 Proof of Theorem 3.1

We outline the proof of Theorem 3.1 in this section. Define $z_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}=(1,x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}})$ . Note that the OLS estimates $\hat{\alpha}^{(1)}$ , $\hat{\beta}^{(1)}$ are unique with high probability if the matrix $M=\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}z_{i}z_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}$ is invertible.

Observe that the $\{A_{i}:1\leq i\leq n\}$ are iid random variables, with $\mathbb{P}[A_{i}=1]=\sigma(x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta)$ . First, observe that an equivalent construction of these Bernoulli variables can be accomplished as follows: let $U_{1},\cdots,U_{n}\sim U([0,1])$ , and define $\xi_{i}=\sigma^{-1}(U_{i})$ . We have,

$$ \displaystyle\{A_{i}:1\leq i\leq n\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\{\mathbf{1}(x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta>\xi_{i}):1\leq i\leq n\}. $$

Note that given $V:=\sum_{i}A_{i}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle M=\left(\begin{matrix}V&\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\\
\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}&\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\end{matrix}\right), $$

where $w_{i}$ is distributed as $x_{i}|A_{i}=1$ . Formally, for any measurable subset $O\subset\mathbb{R}^{p}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}[w_{i}\in O]=\frac{\mathbb{P}[x_{i}\in O,A_{i}=1]}{\mathbb{P}[A_{i}=1]}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{i}}[\mathbb{P}[x_{i}\in O,x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta>\xi_{i}]]}{\mathbb{E}_{\xi_{i}}[\mathbb{P}[x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta>\xi_{i}]]}. $$

This immediately implies that conditional on $V$ , $w_{i}$ are iid, and their distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. [43] implies that if $V\geq p$ , then $\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}$ is invertible almost surely. Further,

$$ \displaystyle V-\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}\Big)^{\mathrm{T}}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\Big)^{-1}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}\Big)\neq 0 $$

with probability 1, as the concerned random variables have a density with respect to Lebesgue measure. This establishes that $M$ is invertible almost surely if $V\geq p$ . Marginally, $V\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\mathbb{E}[\sigma(x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta)])$ . Thus if $\mathrm{E}[\sigma(\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}Z)]>(1+\varepsilon)\kappa$ , then $V>p$ with high probability. In this case, $M$ will be invertible with high probability. Direct calculation reveals that $\mathbb{E}[\sigma(\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}Z)]=\frac{1}{2}$ . An analogous computation applies for the OLS estimates $(\hat{\alpha}^{(0)},\hat{\beta}^{(0)})$ , as

$$ \displaystyle 1-\mathbb{E}[\sigma(x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta)]=\mathbb{E}[\sigma(-x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta)]=\mathbb{E}[\sigma(x_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}\beta)]. $$

Conversely, if $\mathbb{E}[\sigma(\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}}{\sqrt{n}}Z)]<(1-\varepsilon)\kappa$ , then $V<p-1$ with high probability, and then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}w_{i}^{\mathrm{T}}-\frac{1}{n}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}\Big)\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{V}w_{i}\Big)^{\mathrm{T}} $$

is singular with high probability. This completes the proof.

#### A.3.1 Comparison with classical formula

We here present a further detailed comparison of our high-dimensional formula with the classical variance formula for the AIPW (recall from (8)). Recall from (7) that we expressed our formula as

$$ \sigma^{2}_{\text{cf}}=\left[\left(\sigma^{(0)}\right)^{2}+\left(\sigma^{(1)}\right)^{2}\right]f(\kappa,\gamma^{2})+\frac{\kappa}{9}\left(\sigma_{0\beta}^{2}+\sigma_{1\beta}^{2}-2\rho_{01}\sigma_{0\beta}\sigma_{1\beta}\right)\Big(\frac{1}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{r_{2}}+\frac{1}{r_{3}}\Big), $$

so formally

$$ f(\kappa,\gamma^{2})=\frac{V_{T_{1}}}{\Big(\sigma^{(0)}\Big)^{2}+\Big(\sigma^{(1)}\Big)^{2}}, $$

where $V_{T_{1}}$ is as defined in (26). We will compare this with the classical variance when the noise variances $(\sigma^{(0)})^{2}=(\sigma^{(1)})^{2}=\sigma_{\varepsilon}$ . Recall from (8) that the classical variance formula is given by

$$ \sigma^{2}_{\text{classical}}=2\sigma^{2}_{\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{1}{\sigma(x_{i}^{\top}\beta)}\Big]+\text{Var}\{x_{i}^{\top}(\beta^{(1)}-\beta^{(0)})\}. $$

In Section 3, we argued that the difference among these lies in their respective first terms. To compare these, we first recall that the first term in $\sigma^{2}_{\text{cf}}$ comes from the random variable $T_{1}$ defined in (25). Note that in a low-dimensional (fixed $p$ , large $n$ ) setting,

$$ \sum_{(a,b,c)\in\mathscr{S}_{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_{c}}}l_{S_{c},S_{a}}^{\top}f(\mathcal{E}_{S_{b}},X_{S_{b}})\xrightarrow{p}0, $$

and similarly for $\tilde{l}_{S_{c},S_{a}}^{\top}\tilde{f}(\mathcal{E}_{S_{b}},X_{S_{b}})$ . So, the first set of terms in $T_{1}$ does not contribute in low dimensions. Now we turn to the terms $\mathcal{E}_{S_{c}}^{\top}V_{S_{c},S_{a}}-\mathcal{E}_{S_{c}}^{\top}\tilde{V}_{S_{c},S_{a}}$ in (25). By definition, $\mathcal{E}_{S_{c}}^{\top}V_{S_{c},S_{a}}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{S_{c}}^{\top}\tilde{V}_{S_{c},S_{a}}$ are independent, which implies that the total contribution from these in $V_{T_{1}}$ equals

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{{(a,b,c)\in\mathscr{S}_{3}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_{c}}}\mathcal{E}_{S_{c}}^{\top}V_{S_{c},S_{a}}\right)=\text{Var}\left(\mathcal{E}_{S_{3}}^{\top}V_{S_{3},S_{1}}\right)+\text{Cov}\left(\mathcal{E}_{S_{3}}^{\top}V_{S_{3},S_{1}},\mathcal{E}_{S_{3}}^{\top}V_{S_{3},S_{2}}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma^{2}\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{1}}}\right)}\right]+\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{1}}}\right)\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{3}}}\right)}\right]+o_{p}(1)\quad\text{in our setting}, \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\sigma\left(x^{\top}\beta\right)}\right]+o_{p}(1)\quad\text{in low dimensions}. $$

Thus, our formula recovers the classical variance in low dimensions. However, under our high-dimensional setting, (28) no longer holds, nor does the last step in (29), thus our regime differs significantly from its classical counterpart.

## C Proof of Lemma B.3

We prove Lemma B.3 in this section. This is one of the main technical contributions of this paper. To this end, we will need some preliminary technical results. We group these preliminary results for the convenience of the reader.

#### Lemma C.1.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $\{\beta\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma\text{ for some fixed positive constant $\gamma$. }$ Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{A_{i}\}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $\sigma(x_{i}^{\top}\beta)$ . Define

$$ O=\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)\right]^{-1},\quad Q=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}. $$

Then for any vectors $a,b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle a^{\top}Ob-a^{\top}Qb \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\right)^{-1}\cdot\left[a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]}{1-\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)} \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left[b^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]. $$

## D Distributional Identities and Probabilistic asymptotics

We collect some elementary probabilistic identities and asymptotic results in this section. These results will be used crucially in the subsequent discussion.

#### Lemma D.1.

Fix any $\gamma>0$ . Let $z$ be a standard normal random variable. Then $\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}\right]=\frac{1}{2}.$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}\right]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}dz+\int_{-\infty}^{0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}dz+\int_{-\infty}^{0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}z^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{1+e^{\gamma z}}\right)dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}dz+\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}z^{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}\right)dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}z^{2}dz=\frac{1}{2}. $$

∎

#### Lemma D.2.

Fix any $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ . Let $x\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n}I_{p})$ , and $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be any fixed vector. Let $A$ be a Bernoulli random variable with success probability $\sigma\left(x^{\top}\beta\right)$ . Then $\mathbb{P}(A=1)=\frac{1}{2}$ .

Since $x^{\top}\beta\sim N(0,\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(A=1)=\mathbb{E}[\sigma(x^{\top}\beta)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sigma(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx+\int_{-\infty}^{0}(1-\sigma(-x))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx+\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\sigma(y))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{y^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dy=\frac{1}{2}. $$

∎

#### Lemma D.3.

For any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , let $x_{1}\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{\beta_{1}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic scalars such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\beta_{1}}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma$ for some constant $\gamma>0$ . Let $A$ be a Bernoulli random variable with success probability $\sigma\left(x_{1}\beta_{1}\right)$ . Then

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\sqrt{n}x_{1}\mid A=1\right]=2e_{\gamma,0}. $$

For any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sqrt{n}x_{1}\mid A=1\right]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sqrt{n}xp(x_{1}=x\mid A=1)dx \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\cdot p(A=1\mid x_{1}=x)p(x_{1}=x)dx=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}2\sqrt{n}x\sigma(x\beta_{1})\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\frac{1}{n}}}e^{-2nx^{2}}dx \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\frac{1}{n}}}\frac{2\sqrt{n}x}{1+e^{-x\beta_{1}}}e^{-2nx^{2}}dx=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{2z}{1+e^{-z\beta_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}e^{-2z^{2}}dz=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{2z}{1+e^{-z\beta_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}\right]. $$

Since

$$ \left|\frac{2z}{1+e^{-z\beta_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}\right|\leq 2|z|, $$

by uniform integrability of the sequence $\left\{\frac{2z}{1+e^{-z\beta_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ we complete the proof of the lemma. ∎

#### Lemma D.4.

For every $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , let $z_{1},z_{2},\ldots,z_{n}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{\beta_{1}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic scalars such that

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\beta_{1}}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma\text{ for some fixed positive constant $\gamma$. } $$

Let $\{A_{i}\}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $\sigma(z_{i}\beta_{1})$ . Then

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}z_{i}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}+o_{p}(1). $$

Since for any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , $\sqrt{n}z_{1}\sim N(0,1)$ , we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|nA_{i}z_{i}^{2}\right|>n\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|nz_{i}^{2}\right|>n\right)=2n\mathbb{P}\left(\sqrt{n}z_{1}>\sqrt{n}\right)\leq 2n\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{n}{2}}}{\sqrt{n}}\rightarrow 0, $$

where the second last step uses the Mills ratio bound.

Further, we have

$$ \frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[n^{2}A_{i}^{2}z_{i}^{4}\mathbf{1}_{\left(\left|nA_{i}z_{i}^{2}\right|\leq n\right)}\right]\leq\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[n^{2}z_{i}^{4}\right]=\frac{3}{n}\rightarrow 0. $$

Hence by weak law for triangular arrays we can obtain that

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(nA_{i}z_{i}^{2}-\mathbb{E}\left[nA_{i}z_{i}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\left(\left|nA_{i}z_{i}^{2}\right|\leq n\right)}\right]\right)=o_{p}(1), $$

which implies

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}z_{i}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[nA_{1}z_{1}^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\left(\left|nA_{1}z_{1}^{2}\right|\leq n\right)}\right]+o_{p}(1)=\mathbb{E}\left[nA_{1}z_{1}^{2}\right]+o_{p}(1). $$

Finally, let $z\sim N(0,1)$ , then by Lemma D.1 we know

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[nA_{1}z_{1}^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sigma(z_{1}\beta_{1})nz_{1}^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sigma(z\gamma)z^{2}\right]+o(1)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{z^{2}}{1+e^{-z\gamma}}\right]+o(1)=\frac{1}{2}+o(1). $$

Thus we have completed the proof of the lemma. ∎

#### Lemma D.5.

Suppose $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa$ for some fixed $\kappa>0$ . For any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , let $x\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n}I_{p})$ . Let $\{\beta\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}},\{\xi\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be two sequences of deterministic vectors such that

$$ \frac{\|\beta\|^{2}}{n}\xrightarrow{}\gamma^{2},\quad\frac{\|\xi\|^{2}}{n}\xrightarrow{}\hat{\gamma}^{2},\quad\text{ where }\gamma,\hat{\gamma}\text{ are constants}. $$

Then the sequence $\left\{\frac{\left(1+e^{-x^{\top}\xi}\right)^{2}}{1+e^{-x^{\top}\beta}}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ is uniformly integrable.

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left(1+e^{-x^{\top}\xi}\right)^{2}}{1+e^{-x_{i0}^{\top}\beta}}\leq\left(1+e^{-x^{\top}\xi}\right)^{2}=1+2e^{-x^{\top}\xi}+e^{-2x^{\top}\xi}. $$

Since $x^{\top}\xi\xrightarrow{d}N\left(0,\hat{\gamma}^{2}\right)$ , and for any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ , $x^{\top}\xi$ follows a normal distribution, we know that for large $n$ , the variance of $x^{\top}\xi$ is close to $\hat{\gamma}^{2}$ . Hence $\left\{\left(1+e^{-x^{\top}\xi}\right)^{2}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ is uniform integrable, which implies $\left\{\frac{\left(1+e^{-x^{\top}\xi}\right)^{2}}{1+e^{-x^{\top}\beta}}\right\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ is uniform integrable. ∎

#### Lemma D.6.

Fix any $(a,b,c)$ , a permutation of $(1,2,3)$ . Assume the setting described in section 2. Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be any sample in $S_{c}$ . Then the random vector $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x^{\top}\beta\\ x^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\end{array}\right)$ converges in distribution to a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and variance $\Sigma$ , where

$$ \Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}\gamma^{2}&\alpha^{*}_{a}\gamma^{2}\\
\alpha^{*}_{a}\gamma^{2}&\kappa_{a}(\sigma^{*}_{a})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{*})^{2}\gamma^{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$

Conditioned on $S_{a},S_{b}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x^{\top}\beta\\
x^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\end{array}\right)\sim N\left(\mathbf{0},\frac{1}{n}\begin{bmatrix}\|\beta\|^{2}&\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\\
\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}&\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix}\right). $$

By assumption

$$ \frac{\|\beta\|^{2}}{n}\rightarrow\gamma^{2}. $$

Note that $\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}$ is estimated from $S_{a}$ , where $X_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{a}\times p}$ with i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Define

$$ \beta^{{}^{\prime}}=\sqrt{r_{a}}\beta,\quad\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}=\sqrt{r_{a}}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}},\quad X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_{a}}}X_{a} $$

Then $X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{a}\times p}$ with i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n_{a}})$ , and $X_{a}\beta=X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}\beta^{{}^{\prime}},X_{a}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}=X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}$ . Moreover,

$$ \frac{\|\beta^{{}^{\prime}}\|^{2}}{n_{a}}=\frac{r_{a}\|\beta\|^{2}}{n_{a}}=\frac{\|\beta\|^{2}}{n}\rightarrow\gamma^{2}. $$

According to Theorem 4 in [107],

$$ \frac{1}{p}(\beta^{{}^{\prime}})^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}-\frac{\alpha_{a}^{*}}{p}(\beta^{{}^{\prime}})^{\top}\beta^{{}^{\prime}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0,\quad\text{which is equivalent to}\quad\frac{r_{a}}{p}\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}-\frac{\alpha_{a}^{*}r_{a}}{p}\beta^{\top}\beta\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

This implies

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\alpha_{a}^{*}}{n}\beta^{\top}\beta=\alpha_{a}^{*}\gamma^{2}\quad\text{almost surely.} $$

Moreover, applying Theorem 4 in [107] with $\psi(t,u)=(t+\alpha_{a}^{*}u)^{2}$ yields

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}\|^{2}}{p}=(\sigma_{a}^{*})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{*})^{2}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\|{\beta^{{}^{\prime}}}\|^{2}}{p}=(\sigma_{a}^{*})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{*})^{2}\frac{r_{a}\gamma^{2}}{\kappa}\quad\text{almost surely.} $$

Thus

$$ \frac{\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\|^{2}}{n}=\frac{\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{\prime}\|^{2}}{p}\cdot\frac{p}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{r_{a}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\kappa_{a}(\sigma_{a}^{*})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{*})^{2}\gamma^{2}. $$

Hence we know

$$ \displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x^{\top}\beta\\
x^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\end{array}\right)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(\mathbf{0},\begin{bmatrix}\gamma^{2}&\alpha^{*}_{a}\gamma^{2}\\
\alpha^{*}_{a}\gamma^{2}&\kappa_{a}(\sigma^{*}_{a})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{*})^{2}\gamma^{2}\end{bmatrix}\right), $$

which does not depend on $S_{a},S_{b}$ . This completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

#### Lemma D.7.

Assume the setting described in section 2. Then

$$ \frac{1}{n_{c}}\sum_{i\in S_{c}}\left(\frac{A_{i}}{\sigma\left(x_{i}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right)=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]+o_{p}(1). $$

Let $c_{1}$ be the index of any sample in $S_{c}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{A_{c_{1}}}{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]+o(1). $$

Define

$$ S_{n}=\sum_{i\in S_{c}}\left(\frac{A_{i}}{\sigma\left(x_{i}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right). $$

We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]=n_{c}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\beta\right)}{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right], $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{S_{n}-\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]}{n_{c}}\right)^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n_{c}^{2}}\mathbb{E}^{2}\left[S_{n}\right]-\frac{1}{n_{c}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\beta\right)}{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right]-\frac{1}{n_{c}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}^{2}\right]. $$

Note that

$$ \frac{1}{n_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\beta\right)}{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right]=\frac{1}{n_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]+o(n^{-1})=o(1). $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n_{c}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n_{c}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}^{2}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right]\right]=\frac{1}{n_{c}^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in S_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{A_{i}}{\sigma^{2}\left(x_{i}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right]\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\beta\right)}{\sigma^{2}\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right]\right]=\frac{1}{n_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\beta\right)}{\sigma^{2}\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n_{c}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma^{2}\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]+o\left(n^{-1}\right)=o(1). $$

By equation (38) we know

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{S_{n}-\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]}{n_{c}}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1), $$

which implies that

$$ \frac{S_{n}-\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]}{n_{c}}=o_{p}(1). $$

Finally, since

$$ \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[S_{n}\right]}{n_{c}}-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\beta\right)}{\sigma\left(x_{c_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}\right)}\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]=o(1), $$

we have

$$ \frac{S_{n}}{n_{c}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sigma\left(Z_{\beta}\right)}{\sigma\left(Z_{\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}}\right)}\right]+o_{p}(1), $$

which completes the proof.

## E Linear Algebra and Random Matrix Results

#### Lemma E.1.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,1)$ . Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Then $\frac{1}{1-\kappa}I_{p}$ is a deterministic equivalent for $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ .

The Lemma is a special case of Theorem 2.3 in [72], where $z=0$ . ∎

#### Lemma E.2.

Fix any $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ . Let $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be any deterministic vector. Suppose $x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ consists of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ , and $A\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\sigma(x^{\top}\beta))$ . Then $xx^{\top}\sim\left(xx^{\top}\mid A=a\right)\;\;\forall a=0,1.$

Without loss of generality, assume $a=1$ . Let $P$ be an orthogonal matrix whose first row is $\frac{\beta^{\top}}{\|\beta\|}$ . Then we have

$$ P\frac{\beta}{\|\beta\|}=e_{1},\quad A\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\sigma((Px)^{\top}(P\beta)))=\text{Bernoulli}(\sigma(\|\beta\|z_{1})). $$

Define $z=Px$ . Then

$$ xx^{\top}=P^{\top}zz^{\top}P,\quad\left(xx^{\top}\mid A=a\right)=P^{\top}\left(zz^{\top}\mid A=a\right)P. $$

Thus we only need to show $zz^{\top}\sim(zz^{\top}\mid A=1).$ Define $w:=(z\mid A=1)$ . We want to prove $zz^{\top}\sim ww^{\top}.$ Since $z_{j}\perp\!\!\!\!\perp A\;\;\forall j\geq 2$ , we only need to show

$$ (w_{1}^{2},w_{1}w_{2},w_{1}w_{3},\ldots,w_{1}w_{p})\sim(z_{1}^{2},z_{1}z_{2},z_{1}z_{3},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}). $$

We need to show that for any $c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{p}\in\mathbb{R}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(w_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},w_{1}w_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,w_{1}w_{p}\leq c_{p})=\mathbb{P}(z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}\mid A=1) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(A=1\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})\cdot 2\mathbb{P}(z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}\mid A=0) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(A=0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})\cdot 2\mathbb{P}(z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}) $$

Therefore, in order to show equation (39), we only need to show

$$ \mathbb{P}(A=1\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=\mathbb{P}(A=0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=\frac{1}{2}. $$

We know

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(A=1\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(A=1\mid z_{1}=z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sigma(\|\beta\|z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(\|\beta\|z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{0}\sigma(\|\beta\|z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(\|\beta\|z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{0}\left[1-\sigma(-\|\beta\|z)\right]p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz. $$

By a change of variable, we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{0}\left[1-\sigma(-\|\beta\|z)\right]p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\left[1-\sigma(\|\beta\|z)\right]p(z_{1}=-z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz. $$

Further, by symmetry, we have that for all $z\in\mathbb{R},$

$$ p(z_{1}=-z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}). $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(\|\beta\|z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{0}\left[1-\sigma(-\|\beta\|z)\right]p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(\|\beta\|z)p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\left[1-\sigma(\|\beta\|z)\right]p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}p(z_{1}=z\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(z_{1}\geq 0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}). $$

Therefore we only need to prove

$$ \mathbb{P}(z_{1}\geq 0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=\frac{1}{2}. $$

Since

$$ \mathbb{P}(z_{1}=0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=0, $$

we only need to show

$$ \mathbb{P}(z_{1}>0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=\mathbb{P}(z_{1}<0\mid z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}), $$

which is equivalent to show

$$ \mathbb{P}(z_{1}>0,z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=\mathbb{P}(z_{1}<0,z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}). $$

We can assume $c_{1}>0$ , otherwise both sides are equal to 0. Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(z_{1}>0,z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p})=\mathbb{P}\left(0<z_{1}\leq\sqrt{c_{1}},z_{2}\leq\frac{c_{2}}{z_{1}},\ldots,z_{p}\leq\frac{c_{p}}{z_{1}}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{c_{1}}}\mathbb{P}\left(z_{2}\leq\frac{c_{2}}{z_{1}},\ldots,z_{p}\leq\frac{c_{p}}{z_{1}}\mid z_{1}=z\right)p(z_{1}=z)dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{c_{1}}}\mathbb{P}\left(z_{2}\leq\frac{c_{2}}{z_{1}}\right)\cdot\ldots\cdot\mathbb{P}\left(z_{p}\leq\frac{c_{p}}{z_{1}}\right)p(z_{1}=z)dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{-\sqrt{c_{1}}}^{0}\mathbb{P}\left(z_{2}\geq\frac{c_{2}}{z_{1}}\right)\cdot\ldots\cdot\mathbb{P}\left(z_{p}\geq\frac{c_{p}}{z_{1}}\right)p(z_{1}=z)dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(z_{1}<0,z_{1}^{2}\leq c_{1},z_{1}z_{2}\leq c_{2},\ldots,z_{1}z_{p}\leq c_{p}). $$

This completes the proof.

∎

#### Lemma E.3.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $\{\beta\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma$ for some fixed positive constant $\gamma$ . Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{A_{i}\}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $\sigma(x_{i}^{\top}\beta)$ . Then $\frac{2}{1-2\kappa}I_{p}$ is a deterministic equivalent for $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ .

Since

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mathbb{E}\left[A_{1}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\sigma\left(x_{1}^{\top}\beta\right)\right]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sigma(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx+\int_{-\infty}^{0}(1-\sigma(-x))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dx+\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-\sigma(y))\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{y^{2}}{2\frac{\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}}{n}}}dy=\frac{1}{2}, $$

we know that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}=\frac{n}{2}+o(n)\quad\text{almost surely}. $$

For any sequences of deterministic vectors $a,b\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ of unit Euclidean norm, for any $a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}=\frac{n}{2}+o(n)$ , by Lemma E.2 we know

$$ \left(a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\cdot x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b\mid A_{i}=a_{i}\quad\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n\right)\sim a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b $$

Since the trace and the magnitude of the largest eigenvalue of $\sum_{i=1}^{o(n)}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}$ both converge to 0, we know that, almost surely,

$$ \displaystyle a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b=a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{n}{2}+o(n)}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b=a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{n}{2}}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b+o(1) \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\frac{n}{2}}\sqrt{2}x_{i}\cdot\sqrt{2}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{1}\quad b+o(1)=2a^{\top}\frac{1}{1-\frac{p}{n/2}}b+o(1), $$

where the last step is obtained by applying Lemma E.1. Thus

$$ \left(a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\cdot x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b\mid A_{i}=a_{i}\quad\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n\right)-2a^{\top}\frac{1}{1-\frac{p}{n/2}}b\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

This implies that

$$ a^{\top}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}-\frac{2}{1-\frac{p}{n/2}}I_{p}\right]b\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

Similarly, we can show that for any sequences of deterministic matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ with unit operator norm, we have

$$ \frac{1}{n}\text{tr}A\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}-\frac{2}{1-\frac{p}{n/2}}I_{p}\right)\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

This completes the proof.

∎

#### Lemma E.4.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $\{\beta\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\|\beta\|}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma$ for some fixed positive constant $\gamma$ . Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{A_{i}\}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $\sigma(x_{i}^{\top}\beta)$ . Define

$$ P=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top},\quad Q=\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}. $$

Then $\exists c_{p},c_{q}>0$ such that, almost surely,

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{\min}(P)\geq c_{p},\quad\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{\min}(Q)\geq c_{q}. $$

By the main theorem in [100], we have

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{\min}(P)\geq c_{p} $$

for some constant $c_{p}>0$ almost surely.

Moreover, for any $a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}=\frac{n}{2}+o(n)$ , Lemma E.2 implies that

$$ \left(\lambda_{\min}\left(Q\right)\mid A_{i}=a_{i}\quad\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n\right)\sim\lambda_{\min}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}}x_{i}x_{i}^{T}\right) $$

Again, the main theorem in [100] implies that

$$ \lambda_{\min}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}}x_{i}x_{i}^{T}\right)\geq c_{q} $$

for some positive constant $c_{q}>0$ almost surely.

Since

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}=\frac{n}{2}+o(n)\quad\text{almost surely, } $$

we know that, almost surely,

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{\min}(Q)\geq c_{q}. $$

This completes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma E.5.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Then

$$ \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}\kappa. $$

Define

$$ T_{1}=(\sum_{i}x_{i})(\sum_{i}x_{i})^{\top},\quad T_{2}=(\sum_{i}x_{i})(\sum_{i}x_{i})^{\top}-\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i}x_{i}\right)=\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left[(\sum_{i}x_{i})(\sum_{i}x_{i})^{\top}\cdot\left(\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left[T_{1}\cdot\left(T_{1}-T_{2}\right)^{-1}\right]=\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left[I_{p}+T_{2}(T_{1}-T_{2})^{-1}\right]=\frac{p}{n}+\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left[T_{2}(T_{1}-T_{2})^{-1}\right], $$

where the second last step is due to the fact that

$$ \left.(A+B)^{-1}=A^{-1}-A^{-1}B(A+B)^{-1}\right.\text{ for any invertible square matrices }A,B. $$

Hence we only need to show

$$ \frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left[T_{2}(\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top})^{-1}\right]\xrightarrow{p}0. $$

Define

$$ x^{-\{i\}}=\sum_{1\leq j\leq n,j\neq i}x_{j}\quad\forall i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\},\quad x^{-\{i,j\}}=\sum_{1\leq k\leq n,k\neq i,j}x_{j}\quad\forall i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left[T_{2}(\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top})^{-1}\right]=\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left\{\left[\left(\sum_{i}x_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}-\sum_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right]\left(\sum_{j}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right\} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\text{Tr}\left\{\left[\sum_{i}x_{i}\left(x^{-\{i\}}\right)^{\top}\right]\left(\sum_{j}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right\}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x^{-\{i\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\left(x^{-\{i\}}\right)^{\top}(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top})^{-1}x_{i}}{1+x_{i}^{\top}(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top})^{-1}x_{i}}. $$

We show the term above has expectation equal to 0, and variance converging to 0.

For each $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\},$ by conditioning on $x_{i}$ and symmetry we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\left(x^{\{-i\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}{1+x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\left(x^{\{-i\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}{1+x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}\mid x^{\{-i\}}\right]\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x^{\{-i\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{x_{i}}{1+x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}\mid x^{\{-i\}}\right]\right]=0. $$

Hence

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\left(x^{\{-i\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}{1+x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}\right]=0. $$

Moreover, its variance is

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\left(x^{\{-i\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}{1+x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq i}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[n\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}{1+x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}}\right)^{2}\right]\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[n(n-1)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}\right)\left({\left(x^{\{-2\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=2}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}\right)\right]\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[n\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}\right)^{2}\right]\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[n(n-1)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left({\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}\right)\left({\left(x^{\{-2\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}}\right)\right]\right]. $$

We then show both terms on the RHS of (40) converge to 0.

The first term converges to 0 because

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[n\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)^{2}\right]\right] \displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x^{\{-1\}}\cdot\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[x_{1}^{\top}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x^{\{-1\}}\cdot\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right]x_{1}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}{\text{Tr}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x^{\{-1\}}\cdot\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right]\right)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\text{Tr}\left(\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x^{\{-1\}}\cdot\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-2}x^{\{-1\}}\right]. $$

By Lemma E.4 we know there exists a constant $C$ that upper bounds $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\|\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right\|$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-2}x^{\{-1\}}\right]\leq\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}x^{\{-1\}}\right]\cdot C^{2}=0. $$

Now we show the second term on the RHS of (40) also converges to 0:

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[n(n-1)\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(\left(x^{\{-2\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right]\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x^{\{-1\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(\left(x^{\{-2\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}+x_{2}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}+x_{1}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right]. $$

Note that since the term inside the expectation below is an odd function of $x_{2}$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}+x_{1}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right]=0, $$

Similarly, note that the term inside the expectation below is an odd function of $x_{1}$ ). Thus

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right]=0. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}+x_{2}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(\left(x^{\{-1,-2\}}+x_{1}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)\left(x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)\right]. $$

Hence in order to show the second term in (40) converges to 0, we only need to show

$$ x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

By the Sherman–Morrison formula we have

$$ x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}=\frac{x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}{1+x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}. $$

By Lemma E.1, we know the deterministic equivalent of $\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ is $\frac{1}{1-\frac{p}{n}}I$ . Thus the denominator converges almost surely to some constant. Hence we only need to show

$$ x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0. $$

Apply the Sherman–Morrison formula again, We have

$$ \displaystyle x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}=\frac{x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1,2}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}}{1+x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1,2}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}}. $$

Since the deterministic equivalent of $\left(\sum_{j\neq 1,2}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ is also $\frac{1}{1-\frac{p}{n}}I$ , we have

$$ x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1,2}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{p}{n}}x_{2}^{\top}x_{1}+o(1)=o(1)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Thus we have shown

$$ x_{2}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{ a.s. }}}{{\longrightarrow}}0, $$

and this completes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma E.6.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Also, let $z\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ such that $z\perp\!\!\!\!\perp X$ . Then

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\xrightarrow{p}\kappa, $$

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\xrightarrow{p}0. $$

First we show

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}\kappa. $$

We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\mid x_{i}\;\;\forall i\right]\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{Tr}\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{p}{n}=\kappa+o(1). $$

Hence we only need to show the variance converges to 0, which is equivalent to show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]^{2}\right]\rightarrow\kappa^{2}. $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]^{2}\right]= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}z_{i}^{2}z_{j}^{2}\left[x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}\right]\left[x_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{j}\right]\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}z_{i}^{2}z_{j}^{2}\left[x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{j}\right]^{2}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{4}\left[x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}\right]^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\left[x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}\right]\left[x_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{j}\right]\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\left[x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{j}\right]^{2}\right]+\frac{3}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[x_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}x_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{i}\right]^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left[\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)\right]^{2}\right]+o(1)=\kappa^{2}+o(1), $$

where the second last step is due to the fact that

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{2}\right)^{2}\right]=0,\quad\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}\right)^{2}\right]=O(1). $$

Hence

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]^{2}\right]\rightarrow\kappa^{2}, $$

and thus we have proved equation (41). We then show

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}0. $$

Note that by symmetry,

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\right]=0. $$

Hence we only need to show that the variance converges to 0.

Since for any $j\neq k,\;j,k\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[z_{j}z_{k}\cdot x_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{k}\right]=0, $$

we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[z_{j}^{2}\cdot x_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{j}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]. $$

Similar to the previous arguments, we can apply leave-one-out argument to obtain

$$ \displaystyle x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)}{1+x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}x_{1}}=O(1)\cdot x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle O(1)\cdot x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)+O(1)\cdot x_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{1}=o(1). $$

Further, since

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left|x_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\right|\leq\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{\|x_{j}\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\cdot\left\|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right\|, $$

which is upper bounded by some constant, by bounded convergence theorem we have

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(x_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}x_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]=0, $$

which completes the proof equation (42). ∎

#### Lemma E.7.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $\{\beta\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\beta_{1}}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma$ for some fixed positive constant $\gamma$ , and $\beta_{i}=0\;\;\forall i=2,3,\ldots p.$ Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{A_{i}\}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $\sigma(x_{i}^{\top}\beta)=\sigma(x_{i1}\beta_{1})$ . Also, let

$$ y_{i}=\left[\begin{array}[]{llll}x_{i2}&x_{i3}&\ldots&x_{in}\end{array}\right]^{\top}\quad\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n. $$

Then

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)=2\kappa e_{\gamma,0}+o_{p}(1). $$

Fix any $n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ . For any outcome $(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ of $(A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{n})$ , define $s_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)\mid\left(A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right) \displaystyle\sim \displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}w_{i1}y_{i}\right), $$

where $w_{i1}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}(x_{i1}\mid A_{1}=1)\;\;\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n$ .

Further, from the proof of lemma D.3 we can obtain that,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[w_{i1}\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{2z}{1+e^{-z\beta_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}\right]:=c_{n},\quad\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n,\quad\text{where }z\sim N(0,1). $$

Since

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}=\mathbb{E}[A_{i}]+o(1)=\frac{1}{2}+o(1),\quad\text{we have}\quad\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\geq(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n\right)\rightarrow 1\quad\forall\delta>0. $$

Choose any $\delta\in(0,\frac{1}{2}-\kappa)$ . There exists an $N$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}$ is invertible for any $n\geq N$ . Fix any $\epsilon>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}(x_{i1}-c_{n})y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)\right|\geq\epsilon\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}(x_{i1}-c_{n})y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)\right|\geq\epsilon\left|A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right.\right) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}\\
\text{ s.t. }s_{n}\geq(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n\end{subarray}}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}(x_{i1}-c_{n})y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)\right|\geq\epsilon\left|A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right.\right) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}<(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}\\
\text{ s.t. }s_{n}\geq(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n\end{subarray}}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}(w_{i1}-c_{n})y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{i}\right)\right|\geq\epsilon\;\;\forall i\right) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right)+o(1). $$

By Lemma D.1 and Lemma D.3, for any $i=1,2,\ldots,n$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(\sqrt{n}w_{i1})= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[nw_{i1}^{2}\right]-nc_{n}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{2z^{2}}{1+e^{-z\beta_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}\right]-nc_{n}^{2}=1-nc_{n}^{2}\leq 1. $$

Thus similar to the proof of Lemma E.6, we can show that

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{{n}}\left(w_{i1}-c_{n}\right)y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{{n}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{i}\right)=o_{p}(1), $$

which implies

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}\\
\text{ s.t. }s_{n}\geq(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n\end{subarray}}\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}(w_{i1}-c_{n})y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{s_{n}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{i}\right)\right|\geq\epsilon\;\;\forall i\right) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(A_{i}=a_{i}\;\;\forall i\right)+o(1) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\left(\sum_{i=1}^{(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n}(w_{i1}-c_{n})y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{i}\right)\right|\geq\epsilon\;\;\forall i\right) \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\geq(\frac{1}{2}-\delta)n\right)+o(1)=o(1). $$

Hence we have proved that

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\left(x_{i1}-c_{n}\right)y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)=o_{p}(1), $$

which implies

$$ \displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right) \displaystyle=\sqrt{n}c_{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)+o_{p}(1). $$

Since

$$ \sqrt{n}c_{n}=2e_{\gamma,0}+o_{p}(1), $$

and by Lemma E.5,

$$ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)=\kappa+o_{p}(1), $$

we know

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{n}c_{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)=2\kappa e_{\gamma,0}+o_{p}(1). $$

Hence we have completed the proof of the lemma.

#### Lemma E.8.

Let $p,n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ be such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{p}{n}=\kappa\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$ . Let $\{\beta\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}}$ be a sequence of deterministic vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\beta_{1}}{\sqrt{n}}=\gamma$ for some fixed positive constant $\gamma$ , and $\beta_{i}=0\;\;\forall i=2,3,\ldots p.$ Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ consist of i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Let $\{A_{i}\}_{i=1,2,\ldots,n}$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with success probability $\sigma(x_{i}^{\top}\beta)=\sigma(x_{i1}\beta_{1})$ . Also, let

$$ y_{i}=\left[\begin{array}[]{llll}x_{i2}&x_{i3}&\ldots&x_{in}\end{array}\right]^{\top}\quad\forall i=1,2,\ldots,n. $$

For any two sequences of $p$ -dimensional vectors $\{a\},\{b\}$ , define

$$ O_{a,b}=a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\right)^{-1}b, $$

$$ Q_{a,b}=a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle O_{a,b}-Q_{a,b} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left[a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\right]}{1-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)} \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left[b^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\right]. $$

In particular, if $a=b=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}$ , then

$$ O_{a,b}-Q_{a,b}=\frac{8\kappa^{2}e_{\gamma,0}^{2}}{1-2\kappa}+o_{p}(1). $$

Define

$$ U=\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top},\quad V=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{\top}. $$

Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left[a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\right]}{1-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)} \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left[b^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)\right]^{2}}{1-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)}. $$

#### Lemma E.9.

Let $P$ be an orthogonal matrix such that $P\beta=\|\beta\|e_{1}$ . Define

$$ \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{j}y_{j}}{\sigma\left(x_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}\right)}\right)=o_{p}(1). $$

we only need to show

$$ \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}A_{j}y_{j}e^{-x_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)=o_{p}(1). $$

Similar to the proof of Lemma E.7, we only need to prove

$$ \frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)=o_{p}(1),\;\;\text{where}\;\;w_{j}=(x_{j}\mid A_{j}=1)\;\;\forall j\in S_{a}. $$

Note that by symmetry, the expectation of the left hand side is 0. Thus we only need to show its variance converges to 0.

Define

$$ T=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right), $$

$$ T^{\{-b_{1}\}}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right), $$

$$ T^{\{-a_{1}\}}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j=2}^{n_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right). $$

Then by Efron-Stein inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}\left(T\right)\leq O(1)\mathbb{E}\left[n_{b}\left(T-T^{\left\{-b_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}+n_{a}\left(T-T^{\left\{-a_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}\right]. $$

Thus we only need to show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{\left\{-b_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}\right]=o(n^{-1}),\quad\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{\left\{-a_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}\right]=o(n^{-1}). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle T=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)+\frac{1}{n}y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left[\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}-\frac{\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}^{\top}y_{1}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}\right]\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}^{\top}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)\frac{\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}} \displaystyle= \displaystyle T^{\left(-b_{1}\right)}+\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\frac{\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}^{\top}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)\frac{\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}. $$

Denote the deterministic equivalent of $\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}$ as $cI$ for some constant $c$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\frac{\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle O(1)\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=2}^{n_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}y_{j}e^{-w_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)+o(1)\quad\text{a.s.,} $$

(because the left hand side has zero mean and variance converging to zero), we have

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[n\left(T-T^{\left\{-b_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

We then show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[n\left(T-T^{\left\{-a_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[n\left(T-T^{\left\{-a_{1}\right\}}\right)^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{a_{1}}e^{-w_{a_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{a_{1}}\right)^{4}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-4w_{a_{1}}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}}\right]} $$

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}z_{i1}y_{i}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}A_{i}z_{i1}y_{i}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i\neq k,\;i,k\in S_{a}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}A_{k}z_{k1}y_{k}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]. $$
